IELTS WRITING TASK 2, TWO-PART OPINION QUESTION

Explain why businesses increasingly advertise products as new or improved, then judge whether this emphasis on novelty is a positive or negative development.

KEY POINTS

·
Intense competition pushes firms to differentiate similar products. For example, smartphone manufacturers promote minor camera or battery upgrades because rival devices perform almost identically.
·
Advertising responds to consumers' desire for novelty and status. A newly labelled fashion range or limited-edition drink can attract attention and encourage an immediate purchase.
·
The trend can support genuine innovation when companies invest in safer cars, more energy-efficient appliances or more effective medicines to justify claims of improvement.
·
Overall, it is negative because minor changes are often exaggerated, encouraging unnecessary replacement, electronic waste and consumer disappointment. Annual phone releases are a clear example.

SUGGESTED POSITION

Take a mainly negative position. Acknowledge that advertising genuine advances can inform consumers and reward innovation, but argue that businesses more commonly exaggerate superficial changes to increase sales, which promotes wasteful consumption and can mislead buyers.

Introduction
▸

Paraphrase the focus on novelty in modern advertising and state that competition and consumer psychology explain it, while clearly judging the trend as mainly negative.

·
Refer to companies presenting goods as new, improved or different rather than repeating the wording of the question.
·
Preview both causes, pressure from competitors and customers' attraction to novelty.
·
State that genuine innovation is beneficial, but exaggerated novelty claims create greater harm.

Modern companies frequently market their goods as new or improved, largely because...

Body 1
▸

Explain why businesses emphasise newness, focusing on product differentiation and consumers' appetite for novelty.

·
Explain that brands selling similar smartphones, trainers or drinks need a distinctive feature to capture attention in crowded markets.
·
Show how words such as 'new formula' or 'latest model' create urgency and make an existing product appear more desirable.
·
Use annual smartphone launches or limited-edition fashion collections to illustrate how novelty stimulates repeat purchases.

The main reason companies highlight novelty is that it helps their products stand out in...

Body 2
▸

Evaluate the development and prove that its harmful effects generally outweigh its limited benefits.

·
Concede that promoting a truly safer car, more efficient washing machine or better medicine helps consumers recognise useful progress.
·
Contrast genuine advances with minor cosmetic changes, such as a slightly altered phone camera or redesigned packaging being presented as revolutionary.
·
Connect exaggerated claims to unnecessary spending, loss of trust, planned obsolescence and growing electronic or packaging waste.

Although highlighting genuine technological progress can benefit buyers, the broader trend is damaging because...

Conclusion
▸

Summarise the causes and reaffirm that the commercial and environmental harms make the trend predominantly negative.

·
Restate that competition and consumers' attraction to the latest products drive this advertising strategy.
·
Repeat the qualified judgement that honest promotion of substantial improvements is acceptable.
·
End by stressing that superficial novelty should not be used to pressure people into replacing functional products.

In conclusion, businesses stress newness to attract attention in competitive markets, but...

Environment & Ecology

Words and phrases
carbon footprint
total greenhouse gas emissions caused by an individual or activity
Governments are urging citizens to reduce their carbon footprint.
biodiversity
variety of plant and animal life in an ecosystem
Deforestation is one of the leading threats to biodiversity.
deforestation
large-scale clearing of forests
Deforestation in the Amazon has accelerated at an alarming rate.
renewable energy
energy from sources that are naturally replenished (sun, wind, water)
Investment in renewable energy has surged over the past decade.
fossil fuels
coal, oil, and gas. Non-renewable energy sources
Burning fossil fuels releases harmful greenhouse gases.
greenhouse gases
gases (CO2, methane) that trap heat in the atmosphere
Reducing greenhouse gas emissions is critical to limiting global warming.
sustainable
able to be maintained without depleting natural resources
We need more sustainable approaches to agriculture and consumption.
ecosystem
a biological community of organisms and their environment
Human activity is disrupting fragile ecosystems worldwide.
pollution
contamination of air, water, or soil by harmful substances
Air pollution in major cities poses a serious threat to public health.
conservation
protection and preservation of natural resources and wildlife
Conservation efforts have helped to stabilise tiger populations in India.
Go Further
global warming: the gradual rise in the temperature of the Earth caused by human activity
carbon emissions: carbon dioxide released into the air, mainly by burning fuel
environmental degradation: the gradual damage done to the natural world by human activity
natural resources: useful materials found in nature, such as water, timber, oil and minerals
single-use plastics: plastic items designed to be thrown away after being used once
landfill: a site where rubbish is buried under the ground
carbon tax: a charge that companies or individuals pay for the carbon they produce
water scarcity: a lack of enough clean water to meet the needs of a region
extreme weather: unusually severe weather events such as floods, droughts and heatwaves
energy efficiency: using less energy to achieve the same result
Key Collocations
tackle climate change / environmental problems
combat pollution / emissions
mitigate the effects of global warming
preserve natural habitats / wildlife
raise awareness about environmental issues
a pressing environmental concern
cut / curb carbon emissions
deplete natural resources
phase out single-use plastics

"There is growing consensus that governments must…"
"Without urgent action, the consequences could be irreversible."
"Sustainable development must balance economic growth with…"

Spotting Paraphrase

Not a question type, but the skill behind all of them: recognising the same idea in different words.

LESSON 1 OF 12
Spotting Paraphrase: the core skill
Explain this differently
Show me an example
What is it?

This is not a question type you will see printed on the exam paper. It is the skill that every official question type tests. Every IELTS Reading question, whatever its type, tests the same underlying skill: can you tell that a question is describing the same idea as a sentence in the passage, even though almost none of the words match? The passage almost never repeats the question's exact wording. If it did, Reading would just be a word-search.

Explain this differently
Show me an example
Why it matters

Weak readers hunt for matching words and get pulled toward the wrong sentence, or toward a distractor built from the right words in the wrong combination. Strong readers hunt for matching meaning: a paraphrase can change every word and still be correct, or keep half the words and still be a trap.

Explain this differently
Show me an example
Common Ways the Passage Paraphrases a Question
Synonym swap: "rose sharply" ⇄ "increased rapidly".
Word-class change: "the population increased" ⇄ "an increase in population".
Cause/effect reordering: "X led to Y" ⇄ "Y happened because of X" (watch for distractors that reverse which one caused which).
Quantifier shift: "most", "a few", "none", "all" carry very different meanings, and a distractor often swaps one for another.
Hedged vs absolute language: "may reduce symptoms in some patients" is not the same claim as "cures the illness".
Idiom → literal meaning: "caught off guard" ⇄ "unprepared"; "a roaring trade" ⇄ "a successful business".
Numbers restated differently: "fewer than one in ten" ⇄ "the vast majority do not…".
⚠ Trap: a distractor reuses passage words but reverses the meaning (cause↔effect, more↔less) ⚠ Trap: an option adds a claim the passage never actually makes ⚠ Trap: hedged language ("may", "some", "believed") turned into an absolute claim
Explain this differently
Show me an example
How to Practise It
Read the option and the "passage" sentence below it separately, then ask: do they make the same claim, or just share some words?
Underline the words that carry the meaning (verbs, quantifiers, negatives). Not just topic nouns.
Check direction: who is doing what to whom? A reversed cause/effect is the single most common trap.
Check strength: is the passage certain, or hedged with "may"/"some"/"believed"? Match that strength, don't upgrade it.

Sleeping on the job

Academic Reading Test 20, Passage 1, Questions 1 to 6 and 12 to 13

North Americans are not a people of the siesta. There is a tendency to associate afternoon naps with laziness and non-productivity. Latin Americans and some in European cultures take a different view. In Mexico and Greece, for example, it is customary to close businesses between noon and about 4:00 pm – siesta time. Recent studies are showing that if you can take a 15 to 30-minute nap while at work in the afternoon, you’ll be more alert, more energetic, happier doing what you do, more productive and therefore more likely to get ahead. Napping on the job is not yet a trend but there is serious talk in academic circles about the merits of ‘power napping’.

By some estimate, the average American collects an annual ‘sleep debt’ of 500 hours – subtracting from an assumed norm of eight hours a night. Two out of three Americans get less than eight hours of sleep a night during the work week, according to a recent study by the National Sleep Foundation in Washington. Forty percent say they’re so tired that it interferes with their daily activities. Sleep researcher William Anthony, a professor of psychology at Boston University, says fatigue is a significant problem in modern society. He says sleepiness is a leading cause of auto accidents, second only to drunkenness. All that drowsiness costs an estimated $18 billion annually in lost productivity. ‘We have a simple message,’ says Professor Anthony. ‘People should be allowed to nap at their breaks. The rationale is a productivity one – workers are sleepy, and when they’re sleepy on the job they’re not productive.’

Some companies are encouraging sleep at work, primarily for safety. The Metropolitan Transit Authority, which runs the New York subway system and two suburban railroads, is considering power naps for its train operators and bus drivers. Another railway has started letting its train operators take nap breaks of up to 45 minutes but only when trains are stopped at designated spots off the main lines and dispatchers have been notified. Some overseas air carriers permit airline pilots, when not on duty, to nap in the cockpit. Airlines in the United States have not accepted this practice yet.

According to the Encyclopedia of Sleep and Dreaming: ‘There is a biologically-based tendency to fall asleep in mid-afternoon just as there is a tendency to fall asleep at night. Moreover, if sleep the night before is reduced or disturbed for any reason, a nap the subsequent afternoon is not only more likely to occur, but it can also relieve sleepiness and increase alertness.’ The nap zone, documented in numerous studies, is typically between noon and 3:00 pm. Some people power through this natural slowdown with caffeine or sugar but if employers allowed naps, the benefits would be improvements in mood and performance, especially in mid-afternoon. Workers would concentrate better and persevere in tasks longer. Workers commonly sneak naps even without permission but some companies have begun encouraging naps as part of their policies on boosting production. One US distributor is opening a 2,000-square-foot nap facility that provides beds for up to 20 of its 225 workers at a time. A company in Japan sets up tents in business offices, provides eyeshades and ear plugs, and encourages employees to snooze in the middle of the work day. According to Professor Anthony, ‘You’re not going to see napping at traditional types of operations … but in 21st century-style operations, this isn’t going to be a perk. It’s going to have more to do with productivity. Smart employers are understanding that their employees need rest to do their best.’

Some suspect that corporate naptime, like other perks, is just a way to keep people at the office longer. On the other hand, growing flexibility in hours, for some workers, is allowing nap times to become more common. With eleven million Americans telecommuting and another forty million winking out of their bonus full- or part-time, office hours are basically as long as you can stay awake. One thing is sure: longer commutes, more intense, stressful workday and higher production demands are taking a toll. So, with Americans sleeping less and working longer hours, some employers are warming up to the idea that a little nap in the middle of the day can be good for business.

Every answer below depends on a paraphrase of the passage above: find the sentence that talks about the same idea, then check whether it really makes the same claim. For the Yes / No / Not Given statements: Yes means the passage says the same thing in other words, No means it says the opposite, and Not Given means it never says it.

9

According to the passage, which of the following statements is supported by recent research?

Sleeping on the job

Academic Reading Test 20, Passage 1, Questions 1 to 6 and 12 to 13

North Americans are not a people of the siesta. There is a tendency to associate afternoon naps with laziness and non-productivity. Latin Americans and some in European cultures take a different view. In Mexico and Greece, for example, it is customary to close businesses between noon and about 4:00 pm – siesta time. Recent studies are showing that if you can take a 15 to 30-minute nap while at work in the afternoon, you’ll be more alert, more energetic, happier doing what you do, more productive and therefore more likely to get ahead. Napping on the job is not yet a trend but there is serious talk in academic circles about the merits of ‘power napping’.

By some estimate, the average American collects an annual ‘sleep debt’ of 500 hours – subtracting from an assumed norm of eight hours a night. Two out of three Americans get less than eight hours of sleep a night during the work week, according to a recent study by the National Sleep Foundation in Washington. Forty percent say they’re so tired that it interferes with their daily activities. Sleep researcher William Anthony, a professor of psychology at Boston University, says fatigue is a significant problem in modern society. He says sleepiness is a leading cause of auto accidents, second only to drunkenness. All that drowsiness costs an estimated $18 billion annually in lost productivity. ‘We have a simple message,’ says Professor Anthony. ‘People should be allowed to nap at their breaks. The rationale is a productivity one – workers are sleepy, and when they’re sleepy on the job they’re not productive.’

Some companies are encouraging sleep at work, primarily for safety. The Metropolitan Transit Authority, which runs the New York subway system and two suburban railroads, is considering power naps for its train operators and bus drivers. Another railway has started letting its train operators take nap breaks of up to 45 minutes but only when trains are stopped at designated spots off the main lines and dispatchers have been notified. Some overseas air carriers permit airline pilots, when not on duty, to nap in the cockpit. Airlines in the United States have not accepted this practice yet.

According to the Encyclopedia of Sleep and Dreaming: ‘There is a biologically-based tendency to fall asleep in mid-afternoon just as there is a tendency to fall asleep at night. Moreover, if sleep the night before is reduced or disturbed for any reason, a nap the subsequent afternoon is not only more likely to occur, but it can also relieve sleepiness and increase alertness.’ The nap zone, documented in numerous studies, is typically between noon and 3:00 pm. Some people power through this natural slowdown with caffeine or sugar but if employers allowed naps, the benefits would be improvements in mood and performance, especially in mid-afternoon. Workers would concentrate better and persevere in tasks longer. Workers commonly sneak naps even without permission but some companies have begun encouraging naps as part of their policies on boosting production. One US distributor is opening a 2,000-square-foot nap facility that provides beds for up to 20 of its 225 workers at a time. A company in Japan sets up tents in business offices, provides eyeshades and ear plugs, and encourages employees to snooze in the middle of the work day. According to Professor Anthony, ‘You’re not going to see napping at traditional types of operations … but in 21st century-style operations, this isn’t going to be a perk. It’s going to have more to do with productivity. Smart employers are understanding that their employees need rest to do their best.’

Some suspect that corporate naptime, like other perks, is just a way to keep people at the office longer. On the other hand, growing flexibility in hours, for some workers, is allowing nap times to become more common. With eleven million Americans telecommuting and another forty million winking out of their bonus full- or part-time, office hours are basically as long as you can stay awake. One thing is sure: longer commutes, more intense, stressful workday and higher production demands are taking a toll. So, with Americans sleeping less and working longer hours, some employers are warming up to the idea that a little nap in the middle of the day can be good for business.

gases (CO2, methane) that trap heat in the atmosphere

sustainable
able to be maintained without depleting natural resources
We need more sustainable approaches to agriculture and consumption.

a biological community of organisms and their environment
Human activity is disrupting fragile ecosystems worldwide.

contamination of air, water, or soil by harmful substances
Air pollution in major cities poses a serious threat to public health.
conservation
protection and preservation of natural resources and wildlife
Conservation efforts have helped to stabilise tiger populations in India.
Go Further
global warming: the gradual rise in the temperature of the Earth caused by human activity
carbon emissions: carbon dioxide released into the air, mainly by burning fuel
environmental degradation: the gradual damage done to the natural world by human activity
natural resources: useful materials found in nature, such as water, timber, oil and minerals
single-use plastics: plastic items designed to be thrown away after being used once
landfill: a site where rubbish is buried under the ground
carbon tax: a charge that companies or individuals pay for the carbon they produce
water scarcity: a lack of enough clean water to meet the needs of a region
extreme weather: unusually severe weather events such as floods, droughts and heatwaves
energy efficiency: using less energy to achieve the same result
Key Collocations

combat pollution / emissions
mitigate the effects of global warming
preserve natural habitats / wildlife
raise awareness about environmental issues
a pressing environmental concern
cut / curb carbon emissions
deplete natural resources
phase out single-use plastics

Spotting Paraphrase

Not a question type, but the skill behind all of them: recognising the same idea in different words.

LESSON 1 OF 12
Spotting Paraphrase: the core skill

What is it?

This is not a question type you will see printed on the exam paper. It is the skill that every official question type tests. Every IELTS Reading question, whatever its type, tests the same underlying skill: can you tell that a question is describing the same idea as a sentence in the passage, even though almost none of the words match? The passage almost never repeats the question's exact wording. If it did, Reading would just be a word-search.

Explain this differently
Show me an example
Why it matters

Weak readers hunt for matching words and get pulled toward the wrong sentence, or toward a distractor built from the right words in the wrong combination. Strong readers hunt for matching meaning: a paraphrase can change every word and still be correct, or keep half the words and still be a trap.

Explain this differently
Show me an example
Common Ways the Passage Paraphrases a Question
Synonym swap: "rose sharply" ⇄ "increased rapidly".
Word-class change: "the population increased" ⇄ "an increase in population".
Cause/effect reordering: "X led to Y" ⇄ "Y happened because of X" (watch for distractors that reverse which one caused which).
Quantifier shift: "most", "a few", "none", "all" carry very different meanings, and a distractor often swaps one for another.
Hedged vs absolute language: "may reduce symptoms in some patients" is not the same claim as "cures the illness".
Idiom → literal meaning: "caught off guard" ⇄ "unprepared"; "a roaring trade" ⇄ "a successful business".
Numbers restated differently: "fewer than one in ten" ⇄ "the vast majority do not…".
⚠ Trap: a distractor reuses passage words but reverses the meaning (cause↔effect, more↔less) ⚠ Trap: an option adds a claim the passage never actually makes ⚠ Trap: hedged language ("may", "some", "believed") turned into an absolute claim

Check strength: is the passage certain, or hedged with "may"/"some"/"believed"? Match that strength, don't upgrade it.

OPINION ESSAY, ENVIRONMENTAL BENEFITS VERSUS DISADVANTAGES

Decide whether the environmental gains from people flying less, or not at all, are greater than the negative effects on travellers and businesses, then support that judgement with specific reasons and examples.

КЛЮЧЕВЫЕ ПУНКТЫ

·
Lower demand for air travel can reduce carbon dioxide emissions and aviation's additional warming effects, particularly when short European routes are replaced by rail journeys.
·
Individuals may lose convenient access to overseas relatives, holidays and international opportunities, especially where trains are unavailable or journeys involve remote islands.
·
Airlines, airports and tourism dependent regions may lose revenue and jobs, as seen in destinations whose hotels, restaurants and tour operators rely heavily on international visitors.
·
The environmental gains outweigh these costs because climate damage is widespread and long lasting, while many disadvantages can be reduced through video conferencing, improved rail networks and fewer but longer overseas trips.

ПРЕДЛАГАЕМАЯ ПОЗИЦИЯ

Argue that the environmental benefits do outweigh the disadvantages. Acknowledge serious costs for families, airlines and tourism, but explain that these are more limited and manageable than long term climate change, particularly because businesses and travellers can adopt alternatives.

Introduction
▸

Paraphrase the trend towards flying less and give a direct judgement that its environmental value is greater than the resulting inconvenience and economic costs.

·
Refer specifically to both people who reduce annual flights and those who stop flying.
·
State that aviation's climate impact is the main reason the benefits are greater.
·
Avoid claiming there are no disadvantages for travellers or aviation related businesses.

As concern about aviation's contribution to climate change grows, an increasing number of people are limiting or completely avoiding air travel, and I believe the environmental gains are ultimately more significant than the associated personal and commercial costs.

Body 1
▸

Explain how reduced demand for flights can produce meaningful environmental benefits.

·
Connect fewer bookings across large numbers of travellers with airlines eventually reducing flight frequency, rather than suggesting one cancelled ticket immediately cancels a flight.
·
Mention carbon dioxide and the additional warming caused by aircraft emissions at high altitude.
·
Use short haul travel as an example, such as choosing a train from London to Paris instead of flying.

The strongest argument in favour of this development is that collective reductions in flying can lower aviation related greenhouse gas emissions.

Body 2
▸

Present the main disadvantages for individuals and businesses fairly and specifically.

·
Explain that people with family abroad may face longer, more expensive journeys or fewer visits.
·
Identify affected businesses, including airlines, airport retailers, hotels and tour operators.
·
Use an island or tourism dependent destination as an example, where international visitors cannot realistically arrive by rail.

Nevertheless, limiting air travel can impose substantial costs on both passengers and industries that depend on international mobility.

Body 3
▸

Show why the environmental benefits still outweigh the disadvantages and explain how the costs can be reduced.

·
Contrast the global, long term costs of climate change with the more adaptable problems of travel inconvenience and reduced aviation revenue.
·
Suggest video conferencing for routine corporate meetings and high speed rail for short haul journeys.
·
Recognise essential flights, but argue that fewer leisure breaks and unnecessary business trips would still reduce demand without ending international travel.

Despite these drawbacks, they are more manageable than the lasting environmental consequences of unchecked growth in aviation.

Conclusion
▸

Restate the overall judgement while briefly recognising the groups that need support during the transition.

·
Confirm that environmental gains outweigh personal inconvenience and business losses.
·
Do not introduce a new argument such as aviation taxes.
·
Mention adaptation for tourism workers and travellers who lack practical alternatives.

In conclusion, although flying less can inconvenience internationally connected families and harm aviation and tourism businesses, its contribution to limiting climate damage is more important overall.

КЛЮЧЕВЫЕ ПУНКТЫ

·
Lower demand for air travel can reduce carbon dioxide emissions and aviation's additional warming effects, particularly when short European routes are replaced by rail journeys.
·
Individuals may lose convenient access to overseas relatives, holidays and international opportunities, especially where trains are unavailable or journeys involve remote islands.
·
Airlines, airports and tourism dependent regions may lose revenue and jobs, as seen in destinations whose hotels, restaurants and tour operators rely heavily on international visitors.
·
The environmental gains outweigh these costs because climate damage is widespread and long lasting, while many disadvantages can be reduced through video conferencing, improved rail networks and fewer but longer overseas trips.

ПРЕДЛАГАЕМАЯ ПОЗИЦИЯ

Argue that the environmental benefits do outweigh the disadvantages. Acknowledge serious costs for families, airlines and tourism, but explain that these are more limited and manageable than long term climate change, particularly because businesses and travellers can adopt alternatives.

Introduction
▸

Paraphrase the trend towards flying less and give a direct judgement that its environmental value is greater than the resulting inconvenience and economic costs.

·
Refer specifically to both people who reduce annual flights and those who stop flying.
·
State that aviation's climate impact is the main reason the benefits are greater.
·
Avoid claiming there are no disadvantages for travellers or aviation related businesses.

As concern about aviation's contribution to climate change grows, an increasing number of people are limiting or completely avoiding air travel, and I believe the environmental gains are ultimately more significant than the associated personal and commercial costs.

Body 1
▸

Explain how reduced demand for flights can produce meaningful environmental benefits.

·
Connect fewer bookings across large numbers of travellers with airlines eventually reducing flight frequency, rather than suggesting one cancelled ticket immediately cancels a flight.
·
Mention carbon dioxide and the additional warming caused by aircraft emissions at high altitude.
·
Use short haul travel as an example, such as choosing a train from London to Paris instead of flying.

The strongest argument in favour of this development is that collective reductions in flying can lower aviation related greenhouse gas emissions.

Body 2
▸

Present the main disadvantages for individuals and businesses fairly and specifically.

·
Explain that people with family abroad may face longer, more expensive journeys or fewer visits.
·
Identify affected businesses, including airlines, airport retailers, hotels and tour operators.
·
Use an island or tourism dependent destination as an example, where international visitors cannot realistically arrive by rail.

Nevertheless, limiting air travel can impose substantial costs on both passengers and industries that depend on international mobility.

Body 3
▸

Show why the environmental benefits still outweigh the disadvantages and explain how the costs can be reduced.

·
Contrast the global, long term costs of climate change with the more adaptable problems of travel inconvenience and reduced aviation revenue.
·
Suggest video conferencing for routine corporate meetings and high speed rail for short haul journeys.
·
Recognise essential flights, but argue that fewer leisure breaks and unnecessary business trips would still reduce demand without ending international travel.

Despite these drawbacks, they are more manageable than the lasting environmental consequences of unchecked growth in aviation.

Conclusion
▸

Restate the overall judgement while briefly recognising the groups that need support during the transition.

·
Confirm that environmental gains outweigh personal inconvenience and business losses.
·
Do not introduce a new argument such as aviation taxes.
·
Mention adaptation for tourism workers and travellers who lack practical alternatives.

In conclusion, although flying less can inconvenience internationally connected families and harm aviation and tourism businesses, its contribution to limiting climate damage is more important overall.

energy from sources that are naturally replenished (sun, wind, water)

coal, oil, and gas. Non-renewable energy sources

gases (CO2, methane) that trap heat in the atmosphere

sustainable
able to be maintained without depleting natural resources
We need more sustainable approaches to agriculture and consumption.

a biological community of organisms and their environment

pollution
contamination of air, water, or soil by harmful substances

conservation
protection and preservation of natural resources and wildlife
Conservation efforts have helped to stabilise tiger populations in India.
Go Further
global warming: the gradual rise in the temperature of the Earth caused by human activity
carbon emissions: carbon dioxide released into the air, mainly by burning fuel
environmental degradation: the gradual damage done to the natural world by human activity
natural resources: useful materials found in nature, such as water, timber, oil and minerals
single-use plastics: plastic items designed to be thrown away after being used once
landfill: a site where rubbish is buried under the ground
carbon tax: a charge that companies or individuals pay for the carbon they produce
water scarcity: a lack of enough clean water to meet the needs of a region
extreme weather: unusually severe weather events such as floods, droughts and heatwaves
energy efficiency: using less energy to achieve the same result

Что это за навык

Этого вы не увидите напечатанным на экзаменационном листе как отдельный тип задания. Это навык, который проверяет каждый официальный тип задания в Reading. Любой вопрос IELTS Reading, какого бы типа он ни был, проверяет один и тот же навык: способны ли вы увидеть, что вопрос описывает ту же самую мысль, что и предложение в тексте, даже если совпадающих слов почти нет. Текст почти никогда не повторяет вопрос слово в слово. Если бы повторял, Reading превратился бы в простой поиск слов.

Объясните это иначе
Покажите пример
Почему это важно

Слабые студенты ищут совпадающие слова и попадают не на то предложение или на отвлекающий вариант, собранный из правильных слов в неправильном сочетании. Сильные студенты ищут совпадающий смысл: перефразирование может заменить каждое слово и остаться верным, а может сохранить половину слов и всё равно оказаться ловушкой.

Объясните это иначе
Покажите пример
Как текст обычно перефразирует вопрос
Замена синонимом: "rose sharply" ⇄ "increased rapidly".
Смена части речи: "the population increased" ⇄ "an increase in population".
Перестановка причины и следствия: "X led to Y" ⇄ "Y happened because of X" (следите за отвлекающими вариантами, где меняют местами, кто на кого повлиял).
Смена количественного слова: "most", "a few", "none", "all" означают очень разные вещи, и отвлекающий вариант часто подменяет одно другим.
Осторожная формулировка против безусловной: "may reduce symptoms in some patients" это не то же утверждение, что "cures the illness".
Идиома против буквального смысла: "caught off guard" ⇄ "unprepared"; "a roaring trade" ⇄ "a successful business".
Числа, сформулированные иначе: "fewer than one in ten" ⇄ "the vast majority do not…".
⚠ Ловушка: отвлекающий вариант берёт слова из текста, но меняет смысл на обратный (причина↔следствие, больше↔меньше) ⚠ Ловушка: вариант добавляет утверждение, которого в тексте на самом деле нет ⚠ Ловушка: осторожная формулировка ("may", "some", "believed") превращается в безусловное утверждение

Прочитайте вариант ответа и предложение из "текста" под ним по отдельности, затем спросите себя: они утверждают одно и то же, или у них просто есть общие слова?
Подчеркните слова, которые несут смысл (глаголы, количественные слова, отрицания). Не только тематические существительные.

Это не тип задания, а навык, лежащий в основе всех остальных: узнавать одну и ту же мысль, выраженную другими словами.

Выявление перефразирования: базовый навык

Что это за навык

Этого вы не увидите напечатанным на экзаменационном листе как отдельный тип задания. Это навык, который проверяет каждый официальный тип задания в Reading. Почему это важно

Слабые студенты ищут совпадающие слова и попадают не на то предложение или на отвлекающий вариант, собранный из правильных слов в неправильном сочетании. Сильные студенты ищут совпадающий смысл: перефразирование может заменить каждое слово и остаться верным, а может сохранить половину слов и всё равно оказаться ловушкой.

Как текст обычно перефразирует вопрос
Замена синонимом: "rose sharply" ⇄ "increased rapidly".
Смена части речи: "the population increased" ⇄ "an increase in population".
Перестановка причины и следствия: "X led to Y" ⇄ "Y happened because of X" (следите за отвлекающими вариантами, где меняют местами, кто на кого повлиял).
Смена количественного слова: "most", "a few", "none", "all" означают очень разные вещи, и отвлекающий вариант часто подменяет одно другим.
Осторожная формулировка против безусловной: "may reduce symptoms in some patients" это не то же утверждение, что "cures the illness".
Идиома против буквального смысла: "caught off guard" ⇄ "unprepared"; "a roaring trade" ⇄ "a successful business".
Числа, сформулированные иначе: "fewer than one in ten" ⇄ "the vast majority do not…".

Environment & Ecology
Потренировать эти слова
Слова и выражения
carbon footprint
total greenhouse gas emissions caused by an individual or activity
Governments are urging citizens to reduce their carbon footprint.
biodiversity
variety of plant and animal life in an ecosystem
Deforestation is one of the leading threats to biodiversity.
deforestation
large-scale clearing of forests
Deforestation in the Amazon has accelerated at an alarming rate.
renewable energy
energy from sources that are naturally replenished (sun, wind, water)
Investment in renewable energy has surged over the past decade.
fossil fuels
coal, oil, and gas. Non-renewable energy sources
Burning fossil fuels releases harmful greenhouse gases.
greenhouse gases
gases (CO2, methane) that trap heat in the atmosphere
Reducing greenhouse gas emissions is critical to limiting global warming.
sustainable
able to be maintained without depleting natural resources
We need more sustainable approaches to agriculture and consumption.
ecosystem
a biological community of organisms and their environment
Human activity is disrupting fragile ecosystems worldwide.
pollution
contamination of air, water, or soil by harmful substances
Air pollution in major cities poses a serious threat to public health.
conservation
protection and preservation of natural resources and wildlife
Conservation efforts have helped to stabilise tiger populations in India.
Go Further
global warming: the gradual rise in the temperature of the Earth caused by human activity
carbon emissions: carbon dioxide released into the air, mainly by burning fuel
environmental degradation: the gradual damage done to the natural world by human activity
natural resources: useful materials found in nature, such as water, timber, oil and minerals
single-use plastics: plastic items designed to be thrown away after being used once
landfill: a site where rubbish is buried under the ground
carbon tax: a charge that companies or individuals pay for the carbon they produce
water scarcity: a lack of enough clean water to meet the needs of a region
extreme weather: unusually severe weather events such as floods, droughts and heatwaves
energy efficiency: using less energy to achieve the same result
Key Collocations
tackle climate change / environmental problems
combat pollution / emissions
mitigate the effects of global warming
preserve natural habitats / wildlife
raise awareness about environmental issues
a pressing environmental concern
cut / curb carbon emissions
deplete natural resources
phase out single-use plastics
Useful Essay Phrases
"Environmental degradation poses a long-term threat to…"
"The most effective way to combat climate change would be to…"
"There is growing consensus that governments must…"
"Without urgent action, the consequences could be irreversible."
"Sustainable development must balance economic growth with…"
